description: The team of nerds which will become the best team here.
summary:
Ansharky is a cooperative pixel-art game about preparing and flying a mission to the Moon. Four players each take one role - Analyst, Engineer, Astronaut and Flight Dispatcher - and must work together in a shared mission control room: the analyst manages the budget and buys a rocket, the engineer builds science instruments, the astronaut loads the cargo, and the dispatcher picks the mission type, fuels the rocket and launches it during a launch window.

Every launch plays out as a realistic flight based on NASA data: SLS liftoff, Max Q, booster separation and main engine cutoff follow the real Artemis I timeline, while trans-lunar injection, lunar orbit insertion and the powered descent to the Sea of Tranquility follow Apollo 11. After landing, the astronaut walks on lunar terrain built from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data and collects samples, each tied to a real fact from the Apollo missions.

The game turns real spaceflight data into something players can feel and learn from: why fuel, mass and thrust matter, how a Moon mission unfolds step by step, and why teamwork is essential in space exploration.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ansharky is a 2-4 player online co-op game (also playable solo in test mode). The team has 15 in-game days to send as many science missions to the Moon as possible. Each player controls one character and can only use their own workstation:

- Analyst: budget, sponsor reports, buys rockets (9 ships with different thrust, payload and tank capacity).

- Engineer: turns metal into modules - orbital and surface instruments, antenna, solar panels, boosters, extra tanks, crew capsule.

- Astronaut: loads modules onto the rocket within its payload limit, trains the crew, and walks on the Moon after landing.

- Flight Dispatcher: chooses the mission profile (flyby, orbit, landing, landing & return), fuels the rocket and launches it.

A launch only succeeds if the physics checks pass: enough fuel for the profile, thrust greater than liftoff mass x 1.3, payload within limits, an open launch window and good weather. Daily random events (fuel shortages, grants, storms, solar flares) force the team to adapt.

HOW THE FLIGHT WORKS

Every launch plays a cinematic, data-driven flight with subtitles:

1. Ascent - SLS Block 1 liftoff (39.1 MN thrust), Max Q, solid rocket booster separation (T+2:12), fairing and launch abort system jettison, MECO (T+8:04) and core stage separation, following the Artemis I timeline.

2. Earth orbit - 185 km parking orbit at 7.8 km/s, Orion solar arrays, ICPS perigee raise burn.

3. Trans-lunar injection - +3.1 km/s burn and a continuous transfer trajectory over 384,400 km.

4. Lunar orbit (110 km, 1.6 km/s) or a lunar flyby (130 km closest approach, as on Artemis I).

5. Powered descent from 15 km to touchdown at the Apollo 11 landing site (0.67 N, 23.47 E).

6. Moonwalk - the astronaut explores terrain generated from the NASA LRO LOLA elevation profile of the Sea of Tranquility under 1/6 g gravity and collects six samples (mare basalt, highland anorthosite, regolith, drive core tube, orange volcanic glass, seismometer data). Each sample shows a real scientific fact from the Apollo missions and adds science data to the mission score.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Players learn by doing: they experience the trade-offs between mass, fuel and thrust, why launch windows exist, how a real Moon mission is staged, and what scientists learned from lunar samples. Because every role is required, the game builds communication and teamwork skills - the same skills real mission control teams depend on. It is designed for students and anyone curious about space exploration.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Godot Engine 4.5, GDScript

- High-level multiplayer (ENet): server-authoritative game state, role permissions and validated player requests

- Python 3 + Pillow to process NASA data (elevation profile) and generate pixel-art sprites

- FFmpeg to convert the soundtrack to Ogg Vorbis

- Pixel art drawn at 480x270 and scaled up with nearest-neighbour filtering

CREATIVITY

Instead of a quiz or a simulator, the game wraps real NASA numbers inside a co-op party game: the telemetry, timeline and lunar terrain are real, but the fun comes from coordinating four people with different jobs under time pressure. The retro pixel-art style makes the data approachable.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

- Scientific accuracy: flight phases, speeds, altitudes and lunar facts are taken from NASA sources.

- Accessibility: simple controls (WASD + E), English interface, solo test mode.

- Fair multiplayer: the host validates every action so players cannot cheat or crash the game.

- Balance: costs, incomes and events are kept in one data file so difficulty is easy to tune.
